claims.text: W–Ta–V–Cr and W–Ta–V–Cr–Hf refractory high-entropy alloys can serve as structural materials for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
These W-based HEAs are low-activation materials.
Tungsten has a high melting point suitable for plasma-facing applications.
Tungsten provides radiation resistance to the proposed alloys.
The additional refractory elements confer microstructural stabilization, toughening, and low radioactivation.
Near-equiatomic elemental or pre-alloyed powders are suitable initial feedstocks for fabricating the proposed W–Ta–V–Cr and W–Ta–V–Cr–Hf alloys.
Laser powder bed fusion at approximately 100–300 W laser power, 100–300 mm/s scanning speed, and 45–80 μm hatch spacing will produce dense, bulk, near-net-shape parts from the proposed alloys.
Post-process heat treatment at 1200–1600 K will stabilize the microstructures of the proposed alloys.
Fusion plasma-facing materials must tolerate irradiation and particle fluxes at temperatures of at least 1000 K.
The proposed alloys will form stable BCC-based multicomponent solid solutions.
Fine-grained microstructures in these alloys will impede dislocation motion and limit radiation-induced defect clustering.
High configurational entropy and strong lattice distortion inhibit diffusion and defect migration in the proposed alloys.
Inhibited diffusion and defect migration enhance irradiation tolerance and reduce activation relative to traditional tungsten or steel-based materials.
The proposed W-based HEAs will develop fewer irradiation-induced dislocation loops and voids than pure tungsten or steel.
The proposed W-based HEAs will have lower induced radioactivity than pure tungsten or steel.
The proposed alloys will retain high-temperature strength and toughness and thereby extend plasma-facing component lifetime.
Pure tungsten has low fracture toughness and is susceptible to irradiation-environment damage, including blistering, bubbles, pits, and holes.
Steel-based alloys generally have higher activation and degrade more severely at high temperature than the proposed W-based HEAs.
Long-dose, full-scale performance and large-scale manufacturing feasibility of these alloys remain unquantified.
The effects of Hf addition on activation and mechanical performance remain insufficiently characterized.
